title: ST558_Project3_EDA
text:
The Water Potability data set contains water quality metrics for 3,276 water samples. Each observation includes nine physicochemical properties of the water along with a binary label indicating whether the water is safe for human potable or not.
The variables in this data set are:

ph: pH value of the water (0 to 14).
Hardness: Capacity of water to precipitate soap in mg/L.
Solids: Total dissolved solids in ppm.
Chloramines: Amount of Chloramines in ppm.
Sulfate: Amount of Sulfates dissolved in mg/L.
Conductivity: Electrical conductivity of water in μS/cm.
Organic_carbon: Amount of organic carbon in ppm.
Trihalomethanes: Amount of Trihalomethanes in μg/L.
turbidity: Measure of light emitting property of water in NTU.
Potability: Indicates if water is safe for human consumption. (1 = Potable, 0 = Not Potable)




The goal of this exploratory data analysis is to understand the distributions and relationships among the water quality variables, particularly as they relate to Potability(response variable). We want to identify which physicochemical properties differ between potable and non-potable water and assess whether any strong patterns or correlations exist. This EDA will inform the development of a classification model to predict water potability based on these features.

  theme_minimal() 








The histogram shows that potable and non-potable water samples have nearly identical distributions across all nine predictors. Most variables follow a bell-shaped distribution for both classes. Solids is the exception, displaying a right skewed shape with a long tail.


Boxplots by Potability
Boxplots allow us to compare the central tendency and spread of each predictor across potability groups.

  pivot_longer(-potability, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = potability, y = value, fill = potability)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7)+
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Boxplots of Predictors by Potability",
    x = "Potability",
    y = "Value",
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Not Potable" = "#E74C3C", "Potable" = "#2ECC71")) +
  theme_minimal() 








Across all nine predictors, the median, IQR, and whisker lengths are nearly identically between potable and non-potable. solids stands out with a wider spread and more outliers, but both classes behave identically.

title: ST558_Project3_Modeling
text:
In our exploratory data analysis, we investigated the water potability data set, which contains 3,276 water samples and 10 variables. The goal of this analysis is to build a model of predicting potability (whether water is safe for human consumption).
Our EDA revealed that the target variables is imbalanced and that individual predictors do not linearly separate the classes well. Therefore, we will rely on non-linear algorithms using the tidymodels framework. We will evaluate two models: a Classification Tree and a Random Forest, comparing them based on their logarithmic loss(log-loss).

title: ST558_Project3_Modeling
text:
Train/Test Split(70/30, Stratified on Potability)
We use initial_split from tidymodels with thestrata argument to ensure that the proportion of potable vs. non-potable is preserved in both the training and testing sets.

set.seed(123)

# 70/30 split
water_split <- initial_split(water, prop = 0.70, strata = potability)
water_train <- training(water_split)
water_test <- testing(water_split)

# Check proportions
water_train |>
  count(potability) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  potability      n  prop
  <fct>       <int> <dbl>
1 Not Potable  1398 0.610
2 Potable       894 0.390

water_test |>
  count(potability) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  potability      n  prop
  <fct>       <int> <dbl>
1 Not Potable   600 0.610
2 Potable       384 0.390


Both sets maintain approximately the same proportion of potable vs. non-potable samples, confirming that the stratified split worked correctly.

title: ST558_Project3_Modeling
text:
5-Fold Cross-Validation
On the training set, we create a 5-fold cross-validation split. This will be used for model tuning and evaluation.

set.seed(123)

water_folds <- vfold_cv(water_train, v = 5, strata = potability)
water_folds

ST558_Project3_Modeling
text:
Understanding Classification Tree Model
A Classification Tree is a supervised learning algorithm that works by repeatedly splitting the data into distinct groups based on the predictor variables.

title: ST558_Project3_Modeling
text:
Tuning the Classification Tree Model
We will fit a classification treee using the rpart engine, leaving cost_complexity open for tuning.

# Specify the model
tree_spec <- decision_tree(
  cost_complexity = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune()
) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# Create the workflow
tree_wkf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(water_rec) |>
  add_model(tree_spec)   

# Create a tuning grid
tree_grid <- grid_regular(
  cost_complexity(),
  tree_depth(),
  levels = 5
)

Now we tune the model across our 5-fold cross-validation sets. We will evulate performance using log-loss (which measures the accuracy of predicted probabilities).

# Tune the model
set.seed(123)
tree_res <- tune_grid(
  tree_wkf,
  resamples = water_folds,
  grid = tree_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(mn_log_loss)
)

Let’s look at the top 5 hyperparameter combinations based on lowest log-loss:

tree_res |>
  collect_metrics() |>
  filter(.metric == "mn_log_loss") |>
  arrange(mean)

text:
Save Model for API Deployment
We extract the fully trained workflow (fitted on the complete training set) and save it as an .rds file. This file will be loaded by our plumber API script to serve predictions inside our Docker container.

# Extract the finalized, fitted workflow
best_model <- rf_test_fit |>
  extract_workflow()

# Save the model 
saveRDS(best_model, "best_model.rds")
